column2: The Exchange Organisation (SEO) is the market’s referee: it makes the rules and watches over them.
The Tehran Stock Exchange and Farabourse are where shares are bought and sold. Farabourse’s “base market” means the company doesn’t meet all the conditions; be careful.
The commodity exchange shows the prices of products such as steel and petrochemicals, before the company’s own report.
Codal is the official place for company reports, Sejam/Samat records shares and dividend payments, and tsetmc shows prices.
Like a football match: SEO is the referee, the exchange is the pitch, Codal is the official scoreboard, and tsetmc is the live commentator.
Each day the price can only move between a set ceiling and floor. When everyone wants to sell there’s a sell queue, and you may not be able to sell for several days.
Sometimes a share’s ticker is halted and for a while it can’t be bought or sold.
Many companies have a big government or semi-government owner that doesn’t always decide in small shareholders’ favour.
The government has a big effect on product prices, the dollar and taxes.
Like a one-way street at rush hour: even if you want to turn back, you can’t until the traffic clears.
The price chart in Iran’s market, with queues, halts and rumours, is very noisy and misleading.
But the company’s real profit is recorded on Codal every month, and in the long run the price follows profit.
The fundamental method asks how much money the company makes and what it’s worth. Technical analysis asks whether the price goes up or down tomorrow.
To buy a shop, you look at its monthly takings and costs, not at how many people stood in front of its window yesterday.
Nominal return means how many percent your money grew. Real return means how much more you can buy with that money.
If your money grows 40% but prices go up 45%, you’ve actually become poorer.
The right calculation isn’t simple subtraction: divide (1 + return) by (1 + inflation) and subtract 1.
Last year 100 tomans bought 10 loaves of bread. This year you have 160 tomans (a 60% gain) but each loaf costs 14 tomans; so you can buy about 11.4 loaves. You’re only 14% richer, not 60%.
A share must give more than three things to be worth its risk:
1. The risk-free return, such as Akhza or a fixed-income fund.
2. Inflation, so at least the value of your money is protected.
3. The dollar, gold coins and housing; because people move their money between these.
If government bonds pay 30% with no hassle, a share that pays 25% with lots of stress is a bad deal.
A company that can raise its product price when everything gets more expensive is strong against inflation.
A company whose selling price the government holds fixed while its costs rise gets weaker with inflation.
This is the first FIS screen in Iran.
A bakery with free pricing sells bread for more when flour gets expensive. A bakery on the government price can’t, and its profit melts away.
In Iran, financial statement figures aren’t updated for inflation.
Machines bought cheaply years ago are still on the books at the same old price; so their wear-and-tear cost is counted low and profit on paper looks bigger than it really is.
That’s why a company’s “book value” and the P/B ratio are less useful in Iran.
A house you bought 20 years ago for 100 million is still 100 million on the books; but building one like it today costs billions.
In Dr. Khosravani’s view, shares of companies that pay good dividends are the main engine for building wealth.
Gold and silver are for protecting the value of money. According to him gold beats the dollar in the long run and is safer than land for someone who isn’t an expert.
An exchange-traded gold fund means owning gold without worrying about theft or storage; but a fund can also cost more than it’s worth.
A fixed-income fund earning less than inflation is only a place to park money briefly.
Shares are like a fruit tree that bears fruit every year; gold is like a safe that keeps your money’s value but gives no fruit.
A bubble means buying something for more than it’s really worth.
A gold coin’s real value = the weight of pure gold inside × the price per gram of gold. Anything you pay above that is bubble.
In Mordad 1404 he didn’t see the Emami coin as a good option because of a bubble of about 10%.
If the bubble deflates you lose money, even if the gold price stays the same.
If you buy a 100,000-toman concert ticket from a tout for 150,000, you’ve paid 50,000 tomans of bubble. If tickets get cheap on the last day, that 50,000 is gone.
For years Dr. Khosravani has seen silver as more attractive than gold for the long term.
But on condition that you work out its bubble.
In Dey 1404 he estimated silver’s bubble at about 15 to 25%. Work out today’s number yourself.
Even good fruit is a bad buy if you pay twice the market price.
1. Register and verify your identity on Sejam.
2. Choose a broker to get a trading code and an online trading app.
3. Put money into your broker account and buy from the same app.
Documents and steps sometimes change; check first.
It’s like opening a bank account and getting a mobile banking app; only instead of a bank, it’s a broker.
Volume: how many shares changed hands today.
Trading value: how much money moved today (volume × price).
Market value: the price of the whole company (price × the number of all its shares).
High volume in a cheap share may be little money.
Selling 1,000 packs of gum and selling 1,000 cars is the same count, but the money is nothing alike.
Retail means ordinary people; institutional means funds, banks and companies. tsetmc shows each group’s buying and selling separately.
If retail buyers buy more than they sell, people say “retail money has come in”.
“Smart money” means large purchases by certain people before the price goes up.
A buyer strength above 1 means each buyer brought more money, on average, than each seller.
If at an auction a few people arrive with full wallets and the sellers have little, the price will probably go up; but there’s no guarantee.
These board numbers are in his course, but stock selection is done with Codal, not the board.
The board only helps with “when to buy”, and only for a share you’ve already judged to be good.
Smart money also makes mistakes and can be faked; it’s never the only reason to buy.
First you decide which car to buy (Codal), then you look for a day when they sell it cheaper (the board).
